# Functional biology in its natural context: A search for emergent simplicity

## Authors

- Joy Bergelson<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-7893-7387](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7893-7387)) †
- Martin Kreitman<sup>1</sup>
- Dmitri A Petrov<sup>2</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-3664-9130](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3664-9130))
- Alvaro Sanchez<sup>3</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2292-5608](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2292-5608))
- Mikhail Tikhonov<sup>4</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-9558-1121](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9558-1121))

### Affiliations

1. Department of Ecology & Evolution, University of Chicago Chicago United States
2. Department of Biology, Stanford University Stanford United States
3. Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, Yale University New Haven United States
4. Department of Physics, Washington University in St Louis St. Louis United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The immeasurable complexity at every level of biological organization creates a daunting task for understanding biological function. Here, we highlight the risks of stripping it away at the outset and discuss a possible path toward arriving at emergent simplicity of understanding while still embracing the ever-changing complexity of biotic interactions that we see in nature.

## Introduction

The problem is to construct a third view, one that sees the entire world neither as an indissoluble whole nor with the equally incorrect, but currently dominant, view that at every level the world is made up of bits and pieces that can be isolated and that have properties that can be studied in isolation. Both ideologies [...] prevent a rich understanding of nature and prevent us from solving the problems to which science is supposed to apply itself.

- Lewontin, “Biology as Ideology”

Almost without exception, when nuance is mentioned it is because someone is asking for more of it. I argue that [...] demanding more nuance typically obstructs the development of theory that is intellectually interesting, empirically generative, or practically successful.

- Kieran Healy, “Fuck Nuance”

In the study of biology, we seek simplicity to foster understanding. This quest is driven not only by philosophical desire, but also empirical necessity. Nature brings us immeasurable complexity at every conceivable level of organization — ecological communities are composed of interacting networks of dynamically evolving players; populations of species are defined by membership in closely interacting groups competing for shared resources; cell behavior is governed by a myriad of overlapping and intertwined biochemical pathways and cell-cell interactions; gene regulation is carried out by a web of interacting transcription factors, modified by the cellular environment and epigenetic landscape. All are complex interwoven products of evolution, subject to continual change not by a grand designer but by tinkering and chance. To gain insights into this complexity, our solution as biologists has been to simplify, and this has led to great successes. But, as we will argue below, it has also come with a cost.

The first key level of simplification has been to separate function from evolutionary history, and to organize the study of biology into these two distinct pursuits: ‘How do things work?’ and ‘How did they get that way?’. In the pursuit of functional understanding, the next step has been to simplify the system by isolating the organism from its environmental context. The tool of the trade is a lab-bred model organism — reared on defined growth media, isolated from its natural biotic and abiotic environments, stripped of its natural genetic heterozygosity, and removed from daily and seasonal fluctuations. Humanized mouse models — specialized pure-breeding lines carrying human genes, cells, tissues, or organs — serve as a canonical example of the quest to reduce the complexity of a biological system by isolating its individual components.

Simplification has, likewise, been a key to success in evolutionary biology. It is achieved in a different way, however, by separating the study of processes acting on populations over ecological timescales from the consequences of these processes as revealed on phylogenetic timescales. This separation of timescales has been justified by the belief that ecological change can be rapid — wildfires are an extreme example — whereas evolutionary change in response to an ecological challenge, such as increasingly frequent occurrence of wildfire, is a slow and gradual process. As such, the study of evolution has primarily concerned itself with the inference of history. This principle operates even in population genetics, which in theory bridges ecological processes that govern the fitness of individuals, with evolutionary changes in phenotypes of species driven by adaptation. Most of its machinery aims at making inferences about ostensibly slow evolutionary processes from time-frozen snapshots of genetic variation, with the ecological processes being of relevance only in their long-term average behavior. In ecology, this separation of timescales allows the projection of dynamics from the measurement of contemporary interactions, a tactic that sets aside evolutionary processes. The perceived difference in timescales over which ecological and evolutionary processes act has led to the de facto intellectual divorce of the two — their apparent marriage in the many academic departments entitled ‘Ecology and Evolution’ persisting primarily in name alone.

We contend that while powerful, this current modality of experimental simplification — to a single lab strain in a single environment, or to a single species, or to a static timeframe — handicaps our ability to comprehend nature as it actually exists. Biological entities do not exist in isolation but rather have evolved, and continue to evolve, while enmeshed in a network of ever-changing biotic and abiotic interactions. Even our own human body is, in fact, an entire ecosystem of interacting species and evolving somatic lineages (Ley et al., 2006; Martincorena, 2019). As each of these multiple entities evolves, so too does the network of their interactions (e.g. Fiegna et al., 2015; Urban and Skelly, 2006). Function in these systems is intimately linked to eco-evolutionary dynamics and the eco-evolutionary dynamics are, of course, intimately linked to function. There is no separation of timescales, just as there is no separation of the fields of inquiry. It is all one thing, not merely as a philosophical stance but as an entirely practical matter.

While we fully embrace the goal of simplicity of understanding, we argue that this simplicity must come from a source other than system simplification and isolation at the initiation of inquiry. Indeed, stripping experimental systems from their essential eco-evolutionary context not only makes the resulting functional insights less relevant, it can make them positively misleading. We argue that this approach runs the risk of simplifying away the very phenomena we strive to understand; in essence, eliminating the subject of inquiry before the inquiry even begins.

Our aim here is not to engage in an age-old debate between reductionism and holism, nor argue for more context and nuance for their own sake. Instead, we argue that specifically now, with the recent advances in high-throughput measurement and high-performance computing, we might finally be in a position to interrogate biological systems in their fuller eco-evolutionary context, with the goal of exposing the hidden regularities and arrive at an emergent simplicity of understanding. It is essential to embrace this challenge head-on if we are to understand biological function in the appropriate and relevant context, which we furthermore argue is necessary for any practical application.

## Does it matter?

We have suggested that failure to consider eco-evolutionary context can lead us astray in the understanding of biological function. Is there any evidence that it in fact does? We believe that the answer is yes at multiple levels, from individual genes to complex communities of organisms. Indeed, even a cursory survey provides multiple compelling examples. At the lowest level of biological organization, the function of a single gene cannot be understood without regard to environmental context. The fact that approximately 35% of genes in E. coli, perhaps the best studied organism in the lab, have no known function (Ghatak et al., 2019) is certainly not due to lack of effort, but speaks to the difficulty of understanding organisms in isolation. The function of genes that are recalcitrant to mutational knockout analysis in the laboratory can be revealed under their natural biotic conditions (Barbaric et al., 2007; Chanin et al., 2019; Cruz et al., 2016; Hutchison et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2020; Richter et al., 2009; Ruff et al., 2015). It stands to reason that the full elucidation of gene function, regulatory architecture and developmental robustness will require investigation in an organism’s natural environment.

Similarly, the genetic architecture of phenotypic variation cannot be easily understood outside of the appropriate environmental context. For example, the key developmental genes underlying flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana have been carefully dissected in greenhouse and growth chamber experiments. However, when this same species is grown in natural conditions, GWAS experiments reveal that natural variation in flowering is in fact largely due to variation in circadian clock genes (Brachi et al., 2010). It should therefore not be surprising that selective breeding programs performed in one environment fail to improve the yield of crops grown in another environment (Barrero Farfan et al., 2013). In these and many other examples, such as the difficulty of transferring polygenic scores in human GWAS (e.g. Rosenberg et al., 2019), the context matters enough that it changes the answer in entirely practical ways.

We also know that biotic interactions can be key. For instance, microorganisms often require the presence of their ecological partners in order to grow, a suggestion that was made at the dawn of microbiology (Winogradsky, 1935). This is true even for low-diversity enrichment communities formed in minimal media, where the metabolic activities of all co-occurring species dramatically transform the shared environment, thus permitting the growth of taxa that would otherwise be excluded (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018). Studies have also found that our ability to isolate and cultivate soil bacteria is dramatically enhanced by embedding culture chambers in soil, further emphasizing the challenges that exist when we separate an individual species from its biotic context (Chaudhary et al., 2019; Kaeberlein et al., 2002; Nichols et al., 2010). Of course, the biotic context impacts not only survival. There is growing evidence, for example, that many human pathogens only become virulent when in the company of other community members (Hajishengallis and Lamont, 2016; Wiles and Guillemin, 2019). In a similar vein, mycorrhizal fungi rely on associated bacteria in order to provide services to their host plants (Minerdi et al., 2008). In all these examples, species studied in isolation would fail to display the defining functional phenotypes of interest.

Further, one might think that a functional and eco-evolutionary understanding of species interactions could be gleaned from a study of pairwise interactions between two species, such as a host and a pathogen. But, yet again, careful dissection of these interactions in Arabidopsis thaliana has revealed that these host-pathogen dynamics are driven by a diffuse web of many interactions, including co-occurring host species sharing interacting pathogen species (Karasov et al., 2014). The functional repercussions of this can be profound; for example, an investigation of the evolution of immunity has revealed that humans who live in regions of high pathogen diversity carry alleles with a broader efficacy, as has also been predicted by theory (Manczinger et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2016). In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019), and the evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species (Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020). Lastly, we can see that drivers of species interactions can be found at even higher levels of complexity. For example, Parker et al., 2015 found that disease pressure on host species of a grassland community were predicted not only by the abundance of the one host species of interest, a phenomenon that is predictable by two-species models, but also by the phylogenetic diversity of the entire plant community. The importance of community context in this last example is clear and compelling.

These few examples reveal the perils of ignoring ecological and environmental context. The same is true when we ignore evolutionary change, especially when it occurs on the same timescale as the functional and ecological dynamics in which we are interested. Of course, this has been long recognized in the burgeoning field of eco-evolutionary dynamics (Becks et al., 2012; Hairston et al., 2005; Pelletier et al., 2009; Post and Palkovacs, 2009). Here, we emphasize that these dynamics impinge not only on questions of ecology and evolution but also on biological function, as illustrated below (for more examples, see Box 1).

One recent, compelling example revealed that negative frequency-dependent competition amongst strains of malaria, and the selection that follows from this competition, establish a pattern of limiting similarity that makes the community more robust to perturbations (He et al., 2021). This demonstrates how ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience, an important aspect of community function. In this example, the applied relevance is clear - interventions to control malaria must be more prolonged than currently implemented.

The relevance of eco-evolutionary dynamics is especially clear when we consider cancer, which we now understand to be a process of the evolution of competing somatic lineages. Cancer dynamics depend in crucial ways on the ecological dynamics of the complex cellular communities inside the body, involving interactions and cross signaling among multiple dividing, dying and differentiating cell types such as stroma, tumor, and immune cells (Rodrigues et al., 2021). The current interest in studying cancer within the richer biological context of organoids and genetically modified mouse models reflects the realization that cancer is unlikely to be fully understood by studying cell lines in test tubes, instead requiring consideration of the community of interacting and coevolving cells and cellular lineages. We also know now that even targeted cancer therapies impact tumor growth by affecting not just the tumor cells but also the immune system (Deng et al., 2018; Goel et al., 2017). The same is true for the cancer therapies aimed at the immune system that work very differently depending on the genotype of the tumor (Song et al., 2020).

Similarly, the etiology of many viral diseases is at its core an eco-evolutionary process that connects evolutionary dynamics of large viral populations to the shifting ecological landscape of the immune system. The appropriate scale may be within the body (e.g. HIV), or across population(s), and in relation to dynamics that may involve communities of interacting species (e.g. dengue, flu, SARS-CoV-2; Gibb et al., 2020; Gruber, 2017). The ability of HIV to evolve sufficiently quickly to outrun the immune system and maintain resistance is not the context of function - it is function, at least in the sense that this is what causes the disease of immune deficiency. Along these same lines, the ability of viruses to jump from one species to another, evolve an ability to infect, and then spread, is currently responsible for shutting down the economies of the whole world. Again, evolution is the ultimate cause of these problems, not just some extra context and nuance.

## Is it hopeless?

Given this vast complexity, and accepting that it often matters in key ways, how are we to make progress? If it is not effective to simplify our systems at the outset, must we give up the aspiration for simplicity of explanation? As we argue below, not necessarily.

First, complexity at one level of organization in no way precludes simplicity of explanation at a higher level. In fact, microscopically, all biological systems are impossibly complex. Predictable properties can only arise at some higher levels of organization: that is, simplicity is always emergent. Even something as ‘trivial’ as the exponential growth law of a population summarizes a tremendous complexity of microscopic processes of growth and reproduction. The exponential growth is not a property of any member of the population; it is a property of the entire population. Similarly, the enzymatic kinetics of Michaelis and Menten are immeasurably simpler than the microscopic laws of quantum chemistry ‘under the hood’, and our description of cell physiology rarely invokes the latter. At the next level of organization, the simplicity of quantitative phenomenological growth laws (Schaechter et al., 1958) has been ‘a source of wonder and inspiration’ (Scott and Hwa, 2011). Despite the immense underlying complexity of genetic and metabolic regulation, growth laws can be largely explained by a simple, coarse-grained argument of proteome allocation into ribosomal vs. non-ribosomal components (Basan et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010). At higher levels of organization, organismal traits may be predicted from the laws of mendelian genetics, which were originally derived without requiring any knowledge of the molecular or cellular processes from which they emerge and well before we even knew that DNA was the molecular carrier of genetic information. No physiological or molecular knowledge is required either to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or the effects of drift and selection on allele frequency. Importantly, these and other fundamental results of population genetics describe emergent population-level properties, which lack meaning at the level of a single individual organism. Throughout the history of biology, our successes were never about simplifying away the complexity of a system, but about finding the appropriate coarse-graining.

Can simplicity of functional understanding arise also in systems of interacting and co-evolving populations and species? We suggest yes, partly based on conceptual argument and partly as a matter of empirical evidence. Consider the assembly of microbial communities, which typically consist of hundreds or thousands of taxa. At first glance, it would seem impossibly complex. And yet, recent studies illustrate that microbial ecosystems represent an illuminating example of predictable coarse-grained organization. For instance, the microbiomes of different individual bromeliad plants contain highly similar fractions of their metagenomes devoted to respiration, fermentation, methanogenesis, and other metabolic functions despite varying widely in the species they contain (Louca et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2016). A logical conclusion from this observation is that predictable, species-level compositions are not required for generating predictable dynamics at the level of metabolites. Such emergent simplicity arises generically in consumer-resource models (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019), and it is also exhibited by enrichment communities assembled in simple synthetic environments, where ecological sources of variation (e.g. migration, abiotic factors, bottlenecks, etc.) can be controlled (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018). In minimal sugar-limited environments, for example, two dominant metabolic groups are consistently found: One group is made by respiro-fermentative bacteria, which metabolize the lion's share of the sugar, while the second group is made by respirative bacteria, which specialize on the organic acids that are secreted as overflow metabolic byproducts by the former. The ratios of cell counts in each of these two metabolic groups are quantitatively consistent across communities that were started from different species pools in this system (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019). A similar metabolic organization has been found to repeatedly arise in experimental evolution studies that started from a single isogenic strain (Good et al., 2017; Rozen and Lenski, 2000; Treves et al., 1998). For instance, Rosenzweig and colleagues (Kinnersley et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 1994) found that after only 700 generations in a glucose-limited chemostat, an initially isogenic population of E. coli had diversified into an ecosystem composed of four derived strains. One strain had adapted by increasing the rate of glucose uptake, while the others had specialized in the increased overflow metabolic secretions of the glucose specialist.

We highlight this example because it demonstrates elegantly that both top-down selection among a diverse pool of taxa and bottom-up community assembly via evolution from a single genotype lead to communities that predictably assemble into convergent functional structures. This reproducibility can be explained from a metabolic tradeoff that is fundamentally conserved across all kingdoms of life, where fast-growth in sugars is associated with the secretion of overflow metabolites into the environment. The amount of these byproducts produced per unit glucose consumed is governed by the glucose uptake rate: the faster a bacterium metabolizes glucose, the larger the amount of byproducts it releases (Basan et al., 2015). This leads to a tight covariation between the magnitude of both, even for isolates that belong to different genera (Estrela et al., 2020). Genome-scale metabolic models can correctly estimate the ratio of both metabolic groups by making such simple assumptions.

In these examples, predictability was enabled by the fact that metabolism is highly structured, only some solutions are sensible or mathematically possible, and bacterial taxa have been coevolving with each other for eons, making microbial communities very nonrandom. In a similar way, biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints, combined with (co)evolution, might often lead to predictable and, hence, potentially understandable outcomes in other microbial and non-microbial systems. It is our contention and hope that co-adaptation and co-evolution, especially when it comes to functionally important community or individual traits, will be governed by a limited number of driving forces that, when revealed, will allow for a simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.

## Path forward

So what are we proposing? As mentioned at the outset, we do not aim to rehash previous discussions on holism vs reductionism. This is not the conversation we are trying to have: the limitations of a reductionist approach are well established, as is the fact that the tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries, both fundamental and applied, has been due almost entirely to this very approach. Our aim is not to argue that attempts to reconstruct the whole from pieces is futile. Neither are we asking for more and more complexity for complexity’s sake. Instead, we argue two points.

First, we must remember that ‘what the pieces do’ may not be clear when the whole is extracted from its biological context. This, of course, is not a new insight - we all know it to be true. When we design our experiments around simplified environments, it is not out of a belief that the natural context doesn't matter, but as a matter of feasibility. Our point here is that the time is ripe to act upon this knowledge, and eliminate the barriers of technological convenience. This is essential because the tools that we use shape the research that we do, and as we get better and better sequencing, for example, the comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem. The danger is to keep zooming in on the increasingly microscopic details of species in isolation, where the existing street lights shine brightest. We therefore call for redoubling our efforts to develop new technology for high-throughput functional characterization of organisms in natural or semi-natural habitats of growing eco-evolutionary context (Mallard et al., 2020).

Second, if we are to find the right level of coarse graining, it is imperative to pick model systems of ‘appropriate’ contextual richness and with sufficient replication. But how much is enough? At the outset, we cannot know. Thus, we're advocating for model systems that can be integrated into an axis of tunable contextual richness: lab, semi-natural, and natural. As we increase the size and complexity of experimental systems in a controlled manner, we will search for emergent properties that only reveal themselves at higher levels of organization (and at the appropriate coarse-graining). We can attempt to search for these emergent properties in a systematic manner, rather than discovering them by serendipity. Such a concerted effort will benefit from looking across a diverse array of organisms because only then will consistent, and likely robust, emergent patterns become recognizable. This experimental methodology would go hand in hand with the recent calls in theoretical literature for models of ‘appropriate complexity’ (Getz et al., 2018). To make our proposal more concrete, we present a few representative areas in functional evolutionary biology (Box) where such an approach may be applied and plausibly push the field forward.

Finding the appropriate level of coarse-graining remains a matter of art, an art that becomes harder and harder as the systems become more complex. One exciting possibility is that machine learning and AI methods for performing automated variable selection for learning sparse predictive models will prove effective. However, there are no easy solutions here. Just like more data are not yet progress, a bigger computer alone will not suffice: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces and guide our interrogation of biological systems, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology. These approaches will also inform the development of experimental systems in ecology and evolution that capture the appropriate eco-evolutionary context for organismal function, at least to some phenomenological degree.

Many of the most pressing problems facing humanity - from global change, to infectious disease and zoonosis, to cancer - are all problems of eco-evolutionary function. Confronting these problems will require that we build a sufficient understanding that we can predict, and even control, how these systems function as they evolve. These are challenging and yet crucial problems that will require concerted collaboration across currently disparate fields that extend much beyond the traditional boundaries of Ecology and Evolution, and include all branches of Organismal and Functional Biology, as well as Physics, Engineering, Statistics, and Computer Science.

As we have argued, the enterprise of studying organisms in isolation and as static, already evolved entities, while hugely successful, is also profoundly limited. Our belief, which lies in contrast to Jacques Monod’s famous dictum — ‘Anything found to be true of E. coli must also be true of elephants’ — is that much of what one learns about the functional behavior of E.coli in isolation hardly even extends to E.coli in the gut, let alone to elephants in the savannah. The heart of our proposal, here, is thus the creation of a new field of Function of Evolving Systems that focuses on the function of organisms in the communities in which they reside, over periods of time when interactions evolve. It is both exciting intellectually, and essential practically.

claims.claim: Nature brings immeasurable complexity at every conceivable level of organization, including ecological communities, populations, cell behavior, and gene regulation.
claims.source: Nature brings us immeasurable complexity at every conceivable level of organization — ecological communities are composed of interacting networks of dynamically evolving players; populations of species are defined by membership in closely interacting groups competing for shared resources; cell behavior is governed by a myriad of overlapping and intertwined biochemical pathways and cell-cell interactions; gene regulation is carried out by a web of interacting transcription factors, modified by the cellular environment and epigenetic landscape.
claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the complexity observed in biological systems at multiple organizational levels.

claims.claim: The study of biology has been organized into two distinct pursuits: 'How do things work?' (function) and 'How did they get that way?' (evolutionary history).
claims.source: The first key level of simplification has been to separate function from evolutionary history, and to organize the study of biology into these two distinct pursuits: 'How do things work?' and 'How did they get that way?'.
claims.evidence: This describes the historical organization of biological inquiry into functional and evolutionary domains.

claims.claim: Functional biology simplifies systems by isolating organisms from their environmental context using lab-bred model organisms.
claims.source: In the pursuit of functional understanding, the next step has been to simplify the system by isolating the organism from its environmental context. The tool of the trade is a lab-bred model organism — reared on defined growth media, isolated from its natural biotic and abiotic environments, stripped of its natural genetic heterozygosity, and removed from daily and seasonal fluctuations.

claims.claim: Humans who live in regions of high pathogen diversity carry alleles with a broader efficacy.
claims.source: For example, an investigation of the evolution of immunity has revealed that humans who live in regions of high pathogen diversity carry alleles with a broader efficacy, as has also been predicted by theory (Manczinger et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited empirical and theoretical studies on human immunity.

claims.claim: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions.
claims.source: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019), and the evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species (Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on microbial community interactions.

claims.claim: The evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species.
claims.source: In multispecies microbial consortia, important community functions are often the result of higher-than-pairwise functional interactions (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019), and the evolution of species traits is tightly constrained by the network of interactions with co-evolving species (Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on co-evolution.

claims.claim: Disease pressure on host species in a grassland community is predicted not only by the abundance of the host species but also by the phylogenetic diversity of the entire plant community.
claims.source: For example, Parker et al., 2015 found that disease pressure on host species of a grassland community were predicted not only by the abundance of the one host species of interest, a phenomenon that is predictable by two-species models, but also by the phylogenetic diversity of the entire plant community.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study on disease dynamics in plant communities.

claims.claim: Negative frequency-dependent competition amongst strains of malaria and the selection that follows establish a pattern of limiting similarity that makes the community more robust to perturbations.
claims.source: One recent, compelling example revealed that negative frequency-dependent competition amongst strains of malaria, and the selection that follows from this competition, establish a pattern of limiting similarity that makes the community more robust to perturbations (He et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on malaria strain dynamics.

claims.claim: Ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience in malaria.
claims.source: This demonstrates how ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience, an important aspect of community function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the malaria study about the joint role of ecology and evolution.

claims.claim: Interventions to control malaria must be more prolonged than currently implemented.
claims.source: In this example, the applied relevance is clear - interventions to control malaria must be more prolonged than currently implemented.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about practical implications drawn from the malaria study.

claims.claim: Cancer is a process of the evolution of competing somatic lineages.
claims.source: The relevance of eco-evolutionary dynamics is especially clear when we consider cancer, which we now understand to be a process of the evolution of competing somatic lineages.
claims.evidence: This reflects current scientific understanding of cancer as an evolutionary process.

claims.claim: Cancer dynamics depend on the ecological dynamics of complex cellular communities inside the body, involving interactions among multiple cell types.
claims.source: Cancer dynamics depend in crucial ways on the ecological dynamics of the complex cellular communities inside the body, involving interactions and cross signaling among multiple dividing, dying and differentiating cell types such as stroma, tumor, and immune cells (Rodrigues et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a cited description of cancer as an ecological process.

claims.claim: Targeted cancer therapies impact tumor growth by affecting not just the tumor cells but also the immune system.
claims.source: We also know now that even targeted cancer therapies impact tumor growth by affecting not just the tumor cells but also the immune system (Deng et al., 2018; Goel et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on cancer therapy mechanisms.

claims.claim: Cancer therapies aimed at the immune system work very differently depending on the genotype of the tumor.
claims.source: The same is true for the cancer therapies aimed at the immune system that work very differently depending on the genotype of the tumor (Song et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study on immunotherapy effectiveness.

claims.claim: The etiology of many viral diseases is at its core an eco-evolutionary process that connects evolutionary dynamics of large viral populations to the shifting ecological landscape of the immune system.
claims.source: Similarly, the etiology of many viral diseases is at its core an eco-evolutionary process that connects evolutionary dynamics of large viral populations to the shifting ecological landscape of the immune system.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual characterization of viral disease etiology.

claims.claim: The ability of HIV to evolve sufficiently quickly to outrun the immune system and maintain resistance is the function that causes the disease of immune deficiency.
claims.source: The ability of HIV to evolve sufficiently quickly to outrun the immune system and maintain resistance is not the context of function - it is function, at least in the sense that this is what causes the disease of immune deficiency.
claims.evidence: This is an assertion about HIV pathogenesis based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The ability of viruses to jump from one species to another, evolve an ability to infect, and then spread is responsible for shutting down the economies of the whole world.
claims.source: Along these same lines, the ability of viruses to jump from one species to another, evolve an ability to infect, and then spread, is currently responsible for shutting down the economies of the whole world.
claims.evidence: This refers to the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic impact.

claims.claim: Complexity at one level of organization does not preclude simplicity of explanation at a higher level.
claims.source: First, complexity at one level of organization in no way precludes simplicity of explanation at a higher level.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical principle about emergent properties.

claims.claim: Simplicity is always emergent in biological systems.
claims.source: In fact, microscopically, all biological systems are impossibly complex. Predictable properties can only arise at some higher levels of organization: that is, simplicity is always emergent.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about the nature of biological complexity.

claims.claim: Exponential growth law of a population is a property of the entire population, not of any individual member.
claims.source: Even something as 'trivial' as the exponential growth law of a population summarizes a tremendous complexity of microscopic processes of growth and reproduction. The exponential growth is not a property of any member of the population; it is a property of the entire population.
claims.evidence: This is an example of an emergent property in population biology.

claims.claim: The enzymatic kinetics of Michaelis and Menten are immeasurably simpler than the microscopic laws of quantum chemistry.
claims.source: Similarly, the enzymatic kinetics of Michaelis and Menten are immeasurably simpler than the microscopic laws of quantum chemistry 'under the hood', and our description of cell physiology rarely invokes the latter.
claims.evidence: This is an example of emergent simplicity in biochemistry.

claims.claim: The simplicity of quantitative phenomenological growth laws has been 'a source of wonder and inspiration'.
claims.source: At the next level of organization, the simplicity of quantitative phenomenological growth laws (Schaechter et al., 1958) has been 'a source of wonder and inspiration' (Scott and Hwa, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a cited observation about bacterial growth laws.

claims.claim: Despite the immense underlying complexity of genetic and metabolic regulation, growth laws can be largely explained by a simple, coarse-grained argument of proteome allocation into ribosomal vs. non-ribosomal components.
claims.source: Despite the immense underlying complexity of genetic and metabolic regulation, growth laws can be largely explained by a simple, coarse-grained argument of proteome allocation into ribosomal vs. non-ribosomal components (Basan et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a cited theoretical explanation for bacterial growth laws.

claims.claim: Mendelian genetics was originally derived without requiring any knowledge of the molecular or cellular processes from which they emerge.
claims.source: At higher levels of organization, organismal traits may be predicted from the laws of mendelian genetics, which were originally derived without requiring any knowledge of the molecular or cellular processes from which they emerge and well before we even knew that DNA was the molecular carrier of genetic information.
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact about the development of genetics.

claims.claim: No physiological or molecular knowledge is required to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or the effects of drift and selection on allele frequency.
claims.source: No physiological or molecular knowledge is required either to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or the effects of drift and selection on allele frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the independence of population genetics principles from molecular details.

claims.claim: Fundamental results of population genetics describe emergent population-level properties, which lack meaning at the level of a single individual organism.
claims.source: Importantly, these and other fundamental results of population genetics describe emergent population-level properties, which lack meaning at the level of a single individual organism.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of population genetics.

claims.claim: Throughout the history of biology, successes were never about simplifying away the complexity of a system, but about finding the appropriate coarse-graining.
claims.source: Throughout the history of biology, our successes were never about simplifying away the complexity of a system, but about finding the appropriate coarse-graining.
claims.evidence: This is a historical interpretation of scientific methodology in biology.

claims.claim: The microbiomes of different individual bromeliad plants contain highly similar fractions of their metagenomes devoted to respiration, fermentation, methanogenesis, and other metabolic functions despite varying widely in the species they contain.
claims.source: For instance, the microbiomes of different individual bromeliad plants contain highly similar fractions of their metagenomes devoted to respiration, fermentation, methanogenesis, and other metabolic functions despite varying widely in the species they contain (Louca et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on bromeliad microbiomes.

claims.claim: Predictable, species-level compositions are not required for generating predictable dynamics at the level of metabolites.
claims.source: A logical conclusion from this observation is that predictable, species-level compositions are not required for generating predictable dynamics at the level of metabolites.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bromeliad microbiome observations.

claims.claim: Emergent simplicity arises generically in consumer-resource models.
claims.source: Such emergent simplicity arises generically in consumer-resource models (Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019), and it is also exhibited by enrichment communities assembled in simple synthetic environments, where ecological sources of variation (e.g. migration, abiotic factors, bottlenecks, etc.) can be controlled (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited theoretical and experimental studies.

claims.claim: In minimal sugar-limited environments, two dominant metabolic groups are consistently found: respiro-fermentative bacteria that metabolize the sugar, and respirative bacteria that specialize on organic acids secreted by the former.
claims.source: In minimal sugar-limited environments, for example, two dominant metabolic groups are consistently found: One group is made by respiro-fermentative bacteria, which metabolize the lion's share of the sugar, while the second group is made by respirative bacteria, which specialize on the organic acids that are secreted as overflow metabolic byproducts by the former.
claims.evidence: This is a description of observed metabolic organization in microbial communities.

claims.claim: The ratios of cell counts in each of the two metabolic groups are quantitatively consistent across communities that were started from different species pools.
claims.source: The ratios of cell counts in each of these two metabolic groups are quantitatively consistent across communities that were started from different species pools in this system (Estrela et al., 2020; Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited experimental studies on microbial communities.

claims.claim: A similar metabolic organization has been found to repeatedly arise in experimental evolution studies that started from a single isogenic strain.
claims.source: A similar metabolic organization has been found to repeatedly arise in experimental evolution studies that started from a single isogenic strain (Good et al., 2017; Rozen and Lenski, 2000; Treves et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited experimental evolution studies.

claims.claim: After 700 generations in a glucose-limited chemostat, an initially isogenic population of E. coli had diversified into an ecosystem composed of four derived strains, with one strain adapted by increasing glucose uptake rate and others specialized in increased overflow metabolic secretions.
claims.source: For instance, Rosenzweig and colleagues (Kinnersley et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 1994) found that after only 700 generations in a glucose-limited chemostat, an initially isogenic population of E. coli had diversified into an ecosystem composed of four derived strains. One strain had adapted by increasing the rate of glucose uptake, while the others had specialized in the increased overflow metabolic secretions of the glucose specialist.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from cited experimental evolution studies.

claims.claim: Both top-down selection among a diverse pool of taxa and bottom-up community assembly via evolution from a single genotype lead to communities that predictably assemble into convergent functional structures.
claims.source: We highlight this example because it demonstrates elegantly that both top-down selection among a diverse pool of taxa and bottom-up community assembly via evolution from a single genotype lead to communities that predictably assemble into convergent functional structures.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental evolution and community assembly studies.

claims.claim: This reproducibility can be explained from a metabolic tradeoff that is fundamentally conserved across all kingdoms of life, where fast-growth in sugars is associated with the secretion of overflow metabolites into the environment.
claims.source: This reproducibility can be explained from a metabolic tradeoff that is fundamentally conserved across all kingdoms of life, where fast-growth in sugars is associated with the secretion of overflow metabolites into the environment.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation based on fundamental metabolic principles.

claims.claim: The amount of overflow byproducts produced per unit glucose consumed is governed by the glucose uptake rate: the faster a bacterium metabolizes glucose, the larger the amount of byproducts it releases.
claims.source: The amount of these byproducts produced per unit glucose consumed is governed by the glucose uptake rate: the faster a bacterium metabolizes glucose, the larger the amount of byproducts it releases (Basan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a cited finding about bacterial metabolism.

claims.claim: There is a tight covariation between glucose uptake rate and overflow metabolite production, even for isolates that belong to different genera.
claims.source: This leads to a tight covariation between the magnitude of both, even for isolates that belong to different genera (Estrela et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a cited finding about metabolic relationships across bacterial taxa.

claims.claim: Genome-scale metabolic models can correctly estimate the ratio of both metabolic groups by making simple assumptions.
claims.source: Genome-scale metabolic models can correctly estimate the ratio of both metabolic groups by making such simple assumptions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the predictive power of metabolic models.

claims.claim: Predictability in microbial communities is enabled by the fact that metabolism is highly structured, only some solutions are sensible or mathematically possible, and bacterial taxa have been coevolving with each other for eons.
claims.source: In these examples, predictability was enabled by the fact that metabolism is highly structured, only some solutions are sensible or mathematically possible, and bacterial taxa have been coevolving with each other for eons, making microbial communities very nonrandom.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the observed predictability in microbial systems.

claims.claim: Biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints, combined with (co)evolution, might often lead to predictable and understandable outcomes in other microbial and non-microbial systems.
claims.source: In a similar way, biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints, combined with (co)evolution, might often lead to predictable and, hence, potentially understandable outcomes in other microbial and non-microbial systems.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative generalization from microbial systems to other biological systems.

claims.claim: Co-adaptation and co-evolution, especially when it comes to functionally important community or individual traits, will be governed by a limited number of driving forces that will allow for a simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.
claims.source: It is our contention and hope that co-adaptation and co-evolution, especially when it comes to functionally important community or individual traits, will be governed by a limited number of driving forces that, when revealed, will allow for a simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the nature of biological complexity.

claims.claim: The limitations of a reductionist approach are well established.
claims.source: This is not the conversation we are trying to have: the limitations of a reductionist approach are well established, as is the fact that the tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries, both fundamental and applied, has been due almost entirely to this very approach.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the established understanding of reductionism in biology.

claims.claim: The tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries has been due almost entirely to the reductionist approach.
claims.source: This is not the conversation we are trying to have: the limitations of a reductionist approach are well established, as is the fact that the tremendous progress the biological sciences have experienced over the past centuries, both fundamental and applied, has been due almost entirely to this very approach.
claims.evidence: This is a historical assessment of the success of reductionism in biology.

claims.claim: 'What the pieces do' may not be clear when the whole is extracted from its biological context.
claims.source: First, we must remember that 'what the pieces do' may not be clear when the whole is extracted from its biological context.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about decontextualized research.

claims.claim: When we design our experiments around simplified environments, it is not out of a belief that the natural context doesn't matter, but as a matter of feasibility.
claims.source: When we design our experiments around simplified environments, it is not out of a belief that the natural context doesn't matter, but as a matter of feasibility.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the practical motivations for experimental simplification.

claims.claim: The tools that we use shape the research that we do.
claims.source: This is essential because the tools that we use shape the research that we do, and as we get better and better sequencing, for example, the comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem.
claims.evidence: This is a general principle about the relationship between methodology and research direction.

claims.claim: The comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem as sequencing technology improves.
claims.source: This is essential because the tools that we use shape the research that we do, and as we get better and better sequencing, for example, the comparative lack of tools for high-throughput phenotyping is becoming increasingly a problem.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about current technological limitations in biology.

claims.claim: There is a danger of keeping to zoom in on the increasingly microscopic details of species in isolation, where the existing street lights shine brightest.
claims.source: The danger is to keep zooming in on the increasingly microscopic details of species in isolation, where the existing street lights shine brightest.
claims.evidence: This is a metaphorical warning about research bias toward available methods.

claims.claim: New technology for high-throughput functional characterization of organisms in natural or semi-natural habitats of growing eco-evolutionary context is needed.
claims.source: We therefore call for redoubling our efforts to develop new technology for high-throughput functional characterization of organisms in natural or semi-natural habitats of growing eco-evolutionary context (Mallard et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a call for technological development with a citation to related work.

claims.claim: At the outset, we cannot know how much contextual richness is enough.
claims.source: But how much is enough? At the outset, we cannot know.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty in experimental design.

claims.claim: Model systems should be integrated into an axis of tunable contextual richness: lab, semi-natural, and natural.
claims.source: Thus, we're advocating for model systems that can be integrated into an axis of tunable contextual richness: lab, semi-natural, and natural.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed methodological approach.

claims.claim: As we increase the size and complexity of experimental systems in a controlled manner, we will search for emergent properties that only reveal themselves at higher levels of organization.
claims.source: As we increase the size and complexity of experimental systems in a controlled manner, we will search for emergent properties that only reveal themselves at higher levels of organization (and at the appropriate coarse-graining).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed research strategy.

claims.claim: We can attempt to search for emergent properties in a systematic manner, rather than discovering them by serendipity.
claims.source: We can attempt to search for these emergent properties in a systematic manner, rather than discovering them by serendipity.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed methodological improvement.

claims.claim: A concerted effort to find emergent properties will benefit from looking across a diverse array of organisms because only then will consistent, and likely robust, emergent patterns become recognizable.
claims.source: Such a concerted effort will benefit from looking across a diverse array of organisms because only then will consistent, and likely robust, emergent patterns become recognizable.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed research strategy based on comparative approaches.

claims.claim: This experimental methodology would go hand in hand with recent calls in theoretical literature for models of 'appropriate complexity'.
claims.source: This experimental methodology would go hand in hand with the recent calls in theoretical literature for models of 'appropriate complexity' (Getz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This connects the proposed approach to existing theoretical work.

claims.claim: Finding the appropriate level of coarse-graining remains a matter of art, an art that becomes harder as systems become more complex.
claims.source: Finding the appropriate level of coarse-graining remains a matter of art, an art that becomes harder and harder as the systems become more complex.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the difficulty in finding appropriate simplifications.

claims.claim: Machine learning and AI methods for performing automated variable selection for learning sparse predictive models may prove effective in finding appropriate coarse-graining.
claims.source: One exciting possibility is that machine learning and AI methods for performing automated variable selection for learning sparse predictive models will prove effective.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about the potential of AI methods.

claims.claim: More data are not yet progress.
claims.source: Just like more data are not yet progress, a bigger computer alone will not suffice: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces and guide our interrogation of biological systems, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of data alone.

claims.claim: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
claims.source: Just like more data are not yet progress, a bigger computer alone will not suffice: AI can discover phenomenological regularities, but for such regularities to clue us into underlying causal forces and guide our interrogation of biological systems, data-intensive approaches need to be integrated with the eco-evolutionary theory of functional biology.
claims.evidence: This is an argument for integrating computational and theoretical approaches.

claims.claim: Many of the most pressing problems facing humanity - from global change, to infectious disease and zoonosis, to cancer - are all problems of eco-evolutionary function.
claims.source: Many of the most pressing problems facing humanity - from global change, to infectious disease and zoonosis, to cancer - are all problems of eco-evolutionary function.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of major societal challenges as eco-evolutionary problems.

claims.claim: Confronting these problems will require that we build a sufficient understanding that we can predict, and even control, how these systems function as they evolve.
claims.source: Confronting these problems will require that we build a sufficient understanding that we can predict, and even control, how these systems function as they evolve.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the practical requirements for addressing major challenges.

claims.claim: These are challenging and crucial problems that will require concerted collaboration across currently disparate fields that extend much beyond the traditional boundaries of Ecology and Evolution.
claims.source: These are challenging and yet crucial problems that will require concerted collaboration across currently disparate fields that extend much beyond the traditional boundaries of Ecology and Evolution, and include all branches of Organismal and Functional Biology, as well as Physics, Engineering, Statistics, and Computer Science.
claims.evidence: This is a call for interdisciplinary collaboration.

claims.claim: The enterprise of studying organisms in isolation and as static, already evolved entities, while hugely successful, is also profoundly limited.
claims.source: As we have argued, the enterprise of studying organisms in isolation and as static, already evolved entities, while hugely successful, is also profoundly limited.
claims.evidence: This is a summary assessment of traditional biological approaches.

claims.claim: Much of what one learns about the functional behavior of E.coli in isolation hardly even extends to E.coli in the gut, let alone to elephants in the savannah.
claims.source: Our belief, which lies in contrast to Jacques Monod's famous dictum — 'Anything found to be true of E. coli must also be true of elephants' — is that much of what one learns about the functional behavior of E.coli in isolation hardly even extends to E.coli in the gut, let alone to elephants in the savannah.
claims.evidence: This is an assertion that challenges a famous principle in biology, based on the arguments presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The creation of a new field of Function of Evolving Systems that focuses on the function of organisms in the communities in which they reside, over periods of time when interactions evolve, is both exciting intellectually and essential practically.
claims.source: The heart of our proposal, here, is thus the creation of a new field of Function of Evolving Systems that focuses on the function of organisms in the communities in which they reside, over periods of time when interactions evolve. It is both exciting intellectually, and essential practically.
claims.evidence: This is the central proposal of the manuscript.

results.result: Traditional biological research has been organized by separating functional biology from evolutionary biology, with functional biology isolating organisms from environmental context using lab-bred model organisms, and evolutionary biology separating ecological and evolutionary timescales based on the assumption that evolutionary change is slow relative to ecological change.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 accurately describe established methodological approaches in biology. These are well-documented historical and current practices in the field, representing standard knowledge about how biological research has been organized and conducted.

results.result: Biological systems exist as interconnected networks where function is intimately linked to eco-evolutionary dynamics, with no true separation of timescales between ecological and evolutionary processes, and isolating systems from this context can produce misleading functional insights.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by cited empirical evidence. Claims C9-C11 are logical inferences from this evidence and the examples provided throughout the manuscript. The argument is internally consistent and supported by the empirical examples that follow.

results.result: Approximately 35% of E. coli genes have no known function when studied in laboratory isolation, but gene functions that are recalcitrant to knockout analysis in the lab can be revealed under natural biotic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C13 provides a specific statistic from cited research (Ghatak et al., 2019), and C14 is supported by multiple citations demonstrating context-dependent gene function. These claims provide concrete evidence for the importance of biological context in understanding gene function.

results.result: The genetic architecture of phenotypic variation is context-dependent: natural variation in Arabidopsis flowering is driven by circadian clock genes in natural conditions (different from lab findings), selective breeding programs fail across environments, and polygenic scores in human GWAS are difficult to transfer across contexts.
results.evaluation: All three claims are supported by specific citations to empirical studies (Brachi et al., 2010; Barrero Farfan et al., 2013; Rosenberg et al., 2019). These provide concrete examples of context-dependent genetic effects across different organisms and traits.

results.result: Microorganisms often require ecological partners for growth, with metabolic activities of co-occurring species transforming shared environments to permit growth of otherwise excluded taxa, and many organisms including pathogens and mycorrhizal fungi depend on community members for key functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C22 are all supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating biotic dependencies. The evidence spans historical observations (Winogradsky, 1935) to recent experimental work, providing strong support for the importance of biotic context.

results.result: Species interactions extend beyond pairwise relationships: host-pathogen dynamics involve diffuse webs of interactions, human immunity alleles reflect pathogen diversity, microbial community functions result from higher-order interactions, trait evolution is constrained by co-evolving networks, and disease pressure depends on community-level properties like phylogenetic diversity.
results.evaluation: All claims are supported by citations to specific empirical studies (Karasov et al., 2014; Manczinger et al., 2019; Nourmohammad et al., 2016; Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019; Lawrence et al., 2012; Scheuerl et al., 2020; Parker et al., 2015). The evidence demonstrates complexity beyond pairwise interactions across multiple systems.

results.result: In malaria, negative frequency-dependent competition and selection establish limiting similarity patterns that increase community robustness to perturbations, demonstrating how ecological and evolutionary processes jointly determine community resilience and indicating that malaria control interventions must be more prolonged than currently implemented.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by a specific citation (He et al., 2021). Claims C29-C30 are reasonable inferences from this study about the joint role of ecology and evolution and practical implications. The logical connection between the empirical finding and the conclusions is sound.

results.result: Cancer is an evolutionary process involving competing somatic lineages whose dynamics depend on ecological interactions among multiple cell types (stroma, tumor, immune cells), with both targeted therapies and immunotherapies working through complex interactions between tumor cells and the immune system that depend on tumor genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 represent current scientific understanding supported by citation (Rodrigues et al., 2021). Claims C33-C34 are supported by specific citations to studies on therapy mechanisms (Deng et al., 2018; Goel et al., 2017; Song et al., 2020). The characterization of cancer as an eco-evolutionary process is well-supported.

results.result: Viral disease etiology is fundamentally an eco-evolutionary process connecting viral population dynamics to immune system ecology, with HIV pathogenesis resulting from rapid viral evolution outrunning immunity, and viral zoonotic jumps (like COVID-19) having major global economic impacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 represent established knowledge about viral diseases. The characterization of HIV pathogenesis (C36) and reference to COVID-19's economic impact (C37) are factually accurate. The framing as eco-evolutionary processes is a reasonable conceptual synthesis.

results.result: Complexity at one organizational level does not preclude simplicity at higher levels; simplicity in biology is always emergent, as demonstrated by examples ranging from population growth laws and enzyme kinetics to Mendelian genetics and population genetics principles, with biological success coming from finding appropriate coarse-graining rather than simplifying away complexity.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C46 present well-established examples of emergent properties in biology (exponential growth, Michaelis-Menten kinetics, bacterial growth laws with citations to Schaechter et al., 1958; Scott and Hwa, 2011; Basan et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010, Mendelian genetics, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium). Claim C47 is a reasonable historical interpretation. The argument for emergent simplicity is logically sound and well-illustrated.

results.result: Microbial communities exhibit predictable functional organization despite variable species composition: bromeliad microbiomes show consistent metabolic function distributions, enrichment communities consistently organize into two metabolic groups (respiro-fermentative and respirative bacteria) with quantitatively consistent ratios, and similar organization arises through both top-down selection and bottom-up evolution from single strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54 are supported by multiple citations to empirical studies (Louca et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2016; Goldford et al., 2018; Marsland et al., 2019; Estrela et al., 2020; Good et al., 2017; Rozen and Lenski, 2000; Treves et al., 1998; Kinnersley et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 1994). Claim C55 is a reasonable synthesis of these findings. The evidence for predictable emergent organization is strong.

results.result: The reproducible metabolic organization in microbial communities can be explained by a conserved metabolic tradeoff where fast glucose uptake is associated with overflow metabolite secretion, with tight covariation between uptake rate and byproduct production across genera, allowing genome-scale metabolic models to predict community structure based on metabolism being highly structured and bacterial taxa having coevolved for eons.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by citations to empirical and theoretical work (Basan et al., 2015; Estrela et al., 2020). Claim C59 is a reasonable inference about model capabilities given the mechanistic understanding. Claim C60 provides a logical explanation for the observed predictability. The mechanistic explanation is well-supported.

results.result: Biochemical, physiological, and physical constraints combined with co-evolution might often lead to predictable outcomes in other biological systems, with functionally important traits governed by a limited number of driving forces that could allow simpler coarse-grained understanding to emerge.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are speculative generalizations from the microbial examples to broader biological systems. While the logic is reasonable, these are explicitly presented as hopes and contentions rather than demonstrated results. No direct evidence is provided for these generalizations beyond the microbial case studies.

results.result: While reductionism has driven tremendous biological progress, its limitations are well-established, and current experimental simplification is driven by feasibility rather than belief that context doesn't matter; however, tools shape research directions, and the lack of high-throughput phenotyping tools compared to sequencing creates a problematic bias toward studying isolated microscopic details, necessitating development of new technology for functional characterization in natural or semi-natural contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 represent reasonable assessments of the current state of biological methodology and its limitations. Claim C70 is a call for technological development with citation to related work (Mallard et al., 2020). The argument about methodological bias and the need for new tools is logically sound and well-articulated.

results.result: The appropriate level of contextual richness cannot be known at the outset, so model systems should span an axis of tunable contextual richness (lab, semi-natural, natural) to systematically search for emergent properties at higher organizational levels across diverse organisms, aligning with theoretical calls for models of 'appropriate complexity'.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 present a logical methodological proposal for addressing the challenges identified earlier in the manuscript. Claim C76 connects this to existing theoretical work (Getz et al., 2018). While speculative as a research program, the proposal is internally consistent and addresses the problems identified in the manuscript.

results.result: Finding appropriate coarse-graining is difficult and becomes harder with system complexity; machine learning and AI methods may help with automated variable selection, but data and computation alone are insufficient—AI-discovered regularities must be integrated with eco-evolutionary theory to reveal underlying causal forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 present a balanced assessment of computational approaches. The acknowledgment of difficulty (C77), speculation about AI potential (C78), and caution about limitations (C79-C80) form a coherent argument. The emphasis on integrating computational and theoretical approaches is reasonable and well-articulated.

results.result: Major problems facing humanity (global change, infectious disease, zoonosis, cancer) are fundamentally eco-evolutionary function problems that require predictive understanding of how systems function as they evolve, necessitating interdisciplinary collaboration across ecology, evolution, organismal and functional biology, physics, engineering, statistics, and computer science.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are reasonable characterizations of major challenges and the interdisciplinary requirements for addressing them. While these are inferences rather than empirical findings, they follow logically from the examples and arguments presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Studying organisms in isolation as static entities is profoundly limited, with findings from isolated E. coli barely extending to E. coli in the gut (contrary to Monod's dictum); the authors propose creating a new field of 'Function of Evolving Systems' focusing on organismal function within communities over evolutionary timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are summary assessments that follow logically from all the evidence and arguments presented in the manuscript. Claim C86 is the central proposal of the paper. While speculative as a field-creation proposal, it is well-motivated by the extensive evidence and arguments provided throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Recent advances in high-throughput measurement and high-performance computing now enable interrogation of biological systems in their fuller eco-evolutionary context to expose hidden regularities and achieve emergent simplicity of understanding.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 asserts that current technology enables the proposed research approach, but provides no specific evidence about what these technological advances can actually accomplish in eco-evolutionary contexts. The claim is speculative about capabilities rather than demonstrating them. The manuscript does not provide examples of these technologies being successfully applied to achieve the stated goals.
